citation: "KINZIE MANSION AND FORT DEARBORN." — wood engraving, in Benson J. Lossing, The Pictorial Field-Book of the War of 1812 (New York: Harper & Brothers, 1869).
author: Benson J. Lossing (author and illustrator of the Field-Book); the engraver's name is not legible in the copy held here
describes_date: the Kinzie house and the first Fort Dearborn before 16 August 1812, drawn retrospectively
repository: Wikimedia Commons, File:Kinzie_mansion_and_Fort_Dearborn.jpg; the copy held in this repository is chicago/reference/images/chicago/chicago_kinzie_house_fort_dearborn_1812.jpg (catalogued in chicago/reference/images/IMAGE_SOURCES.md)
locator: the whole plate, 960 x 506 px in the copy held here; the caption is lettered under the vignette
rights_note: Published 1869 in the United States, out of copyright by age; Commons holds it as public domain. Granger also sells it (0066529, 0045092); that is a licence for their scan, not a claim on the 1869 plate.
access_notes: Read off the image file itself on 2026-10-15 (T-2497). The volume's page for this plate was not reached from the run's container, so no page is cited.
what_it_supplies: a long, low, single-storey house on the north bank, its ridge parallel to the river, gables at its ends
a piazza across its front on square posts, under a flatter roof hung below the main eave
two stacks rising through the ridge, one about 0.4 of it from the west gable and one near the west gable
a low picket fence before the house enclosing a green to the water, and a row of tall columnar poplars beside it
a large broad-crowned tree behind the house at the west end
the first fort's picket line and blockhouses across the river, which is what the plate claims to date
what_it_does_not_supply: any dimension or position: it is a tier-5 retrospective view, form only
an eyewitness: Lossing drew it more than fifty years after the fort burned, and his sources for it are not stated on the plate
note: The one picture of the house that claims 1812, by setting it against the first fort. It is retrospective and governs the 1812 house's form only where the other pictures, which show it about 1832-1833, agree with it or say nothing.
